title: Athens Debuts With Interdisciplinary Film Festival Combining AI, Art, And Fashion
text:
By: Giannis Bairaktaris and Christos Makridis
Following two years of closure due to Covid-19, the Athens Fashion Film Festival (AFFF) returned on March 14th for the fourth year with an interdisciplinary theme of “Art-istic OR Art-ificial?" held at the Athens Conservatory under the leadership of Nicole Alexandropoulou. Following an opening ceremony and remarks from Patrizia Falcinelli, the ambassador of Italy to Greece, the festival brought together people from different creative and scientific disciplines.
Art-istic OR Art-ificial?
One of the most interesting discussions took place on the second day of the festival. The roundtable examining the central theme of the 4th AFFF "Art-istic OR Art-ificial?: Artificial Intelligence in Human Creativity” presented the results of a workshop that students from the Creative Fashion Design and the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering of the National Technical University of Athens collaborated on to build designs with AI and traditional tools.
In setting the stage for the roundtable, Nicole Alexandropoulou remarked that “AI can help you in planning and forecasting around the commercial dimension and marketing… you can reduce the waste in production and compress the time it takes to build.” In many ways, AI is an extension of existing technological advances, which have been linked with improvements in employee well-being, according to research published in the journal Technological Forecasting and Social Change.
“Another benefit is that AI can offer alternatives that the creator hasn't thought of. Through the panel at our festival, I realized that the audience is very interested in this new reality. What they were most interested in is how AI can ultimately be a tool to support human creativity hopefully not replace it,” Alexandropoulou continued.
The roundtable explored not only the current, but also the future applications of AI in the realm of artistic productivity, with a particular emphasis on fashion. The students who took part in the workshop and crafted their projects both manually and with tools like DALL-E and Midjourney expressed that AI provides benefits, including: quickness, user-friendliness, and a range of creative concepts. They emphasized that the "artist" remains in charge, as they establish the guidelines for the system to follow.
The results were evaluated and commented upon in a discussion by the workshop organizers: Orsalia Parthenis, fashion designer and artistic director, and Giorgos Stamou, professor at the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering of the National Technical University of Athens, together with the artist Kyriaki Goni.
Recognizing that the artistic and cultural sectors, face the growing influence of AI, the panel began by exploring whether machines can eventually replace human creativity. However, according to Giorgos Stamou “AI is not synonymous with creation; rather, it pertains to production and execution.”
However, the roundtable discussion made clear that peoples’ perception of creative ownership must also evolve. “Creation must presuppose independence, but how different are you when you use the machine, what does it mean for work to be original, and will too much variety eventually bring us to homogenization… these will be answered gradually,” said Orsalia Parthenis.
Much like people use cars to get from one location to another, and thus do not take credit for walking long distances anymore, people may also get more comfortable using AI to augment their creative production. In this sense, the artist must define how the machine will work, rather than let external conditions dictate their creative process.
The conversation revealed that many of the concerns about AI are rooted in the fear of humans losing their creative ownership with the complexity and automation of AI systems. Even if the legal ownership of the created work is clear, the question remains whether those in the arts and culture sectors feel comfortable ceding some of their creative control over to algorithms. “Issues like these were raised with very keen interest from the crowd. It is our wish to delve deeper next year, as we do every year at this festival,” Alexandropoulou continued.
Nevertheless, there are some broader socio-political challenges ahead before the arts can fully leverage AI models. “Unfortunately the data is held by some companies as an oligopoly… the data must be returned to citizens: we first have to claim ownership of the data that belongs to us, and then we have to look at the bias,” said Giorgos Stamou.
Warning of the dangers to removing humans from the creative process, Stamou continued: “Creativity comes from the diversity of human life and emotion… if man leaves experience, diversity will disappear, and machines will bring homogenization. The artist with his experience must define how the machine will work, not the other way round.”
While artificial intelligence is a powerful tool, it cannot entirely substitute human creativity – at least not now. “In my view, while machines may emerge as a significant factor in the creation process, the artist's perspective will always remain crucial, as the act of creation demands both empathy and experience that only a human touch can provide”, Alexandropoulou concluded. Future years of the AFFF are bound to provide similarly engaging and thoughtful discussions and expressions of talent in fashion, art, technology, and beyond.

title: Your next job interview could be judged by AI. Here’s how to prepare.
text:
You may know that artificial intelligence may scan your résumé when you apply for a job. But are you prepared to have an interview assessed by AI?
Here’s how these AI interviews typically work: Candidates are presented questions, either in text or from a recording created by the employer or software company, one at a time. The system records their video responses, often giving them a time limit, usually from one to a few minutes. Some employers allow candidates to rerecord some answers. When the interview is submitted, the AI takes over, analyzing the video for specific skills or traits and providing scores and insights to employers. Candidates are usually told that AI will be used to assess their interview.
Work experts say employers mostly use the technology for openings that draw large numbers of candidates or to help fill hundreds of jobs at a time. Some use it for entry-level candidates whose résumés may lack relevant experience. While some companies, often large employers, have been using AI-assisted interviews for years, the technology is still not widely adopted, according to Rania Stewart, recruiting technology analyst at market research firm Gartner. Between 20 percent and 50 percent of organizations globally are using AI in some part of the hiring process, Gartner estimates. But that could change as AI gets better and companies get more comfortable with using it.
“AI is really becoming more applicable across the board,” Stewart said. AI-assessed interviews are “a high-growth [option] that’s evolving.”
But the technology isn’t perfect. Experts worry that AI could unfairly penalize candidates if it can’t understand a person’s accent or speech impediment, for example. They also worry that it may unfairly score someone who’s neurodivergent or speaks English as a second language.
Software providers say they’re continuously working on improvements to try to eliminate potential discrimination.
Still, experts say there are some things you can do to improve your chances in an AI interview.
“Don’t let yourself be intimidated,” said Marcie Kirk Holland, executive director of the Internship and Career Center at the University of California, Davis. “The locus of control is still with the individual.”
Here are some tips to navigate your next AI interview.
Make sure the focus of your interview is on you. Tech and setup problems could not only affect an AI assessment but also impact your job prospects should a human end up watching the recording.
So ensure you have a strong WiFi connection, your device is plugged into a power source, you have good lighting that doesn’t shadow your face, a flattering camera angle, a properly working webcam and microphone (even if they’re just the ones built into your device) and a clean background. Check that you have the latest updates to your operating system and web browser, as some software has requirements.
Kick out roommates or people who may be in your space disrupting the video. Pick a spot that’s quiet to ensure the software catches everything you say.
“It’s a lot of the same kinds of things we would advise for any interview,” Kirk Holland said.
If AI is assessing your interview, then it shouldn’t matter what you wear or do during it, right?
Wrong. Some AI assessments also take into account what you’re wearing. Dressing professionally not only helps make a good-looking video, but it may put you in the correct head space, too, said Kirk Holland. Avoid multitasking so you don’t lose focus or create audio interference, which could ultimately mess up the AI assessment.
Some employers double back after the AI assessment and watch some videos to ultimately determine who moves on. You don’t want to be caught in your pajamas if that happens.
The software “just provides a score … and [employers] can review the videos and agree or disagree,” said Eric Sydell, executive vice president of innovation at Modern Hire, which offers AI-assessed interviews.
As with any interview, do your research ahead of time. Make sure that not only is a job and employer a fit for you, but that you know what they’re looking for and what to expect.
Kirk Holland suggests job seekers check review sites such as Glassdoor as well as LinkedIn. This will help you get a better idea of how current employees, customers and partners view and work with the company. It also should give you a sense of what the company values and their expectations for workers. Take notes.
If you’re applying to several jobs at a time, your research will help you remember which is which, Kirk Holland said.
“It can all blur together,” she said. “So have really clear records.”
Often times, AI-assessed interviews ask similar questions, experts and software providers said. So prepare what you want to say.
A common question employers ask in AI-assessed interviews is to describe your experience in a specific capacity. The interviews often also include situational questions, such as, “Tell us about a time you solved a tough problem.”
HireVue, a software provider that offers AI interviews, says its system looks for both job abilities and soft skills like communication, problem-solving skills, team orientation and initiative. Other providers, such as Interview.ai, focus more on attitude, professionalism, communication and sociability — using other tools to assess job skills. And Modern Hire says it scores on 11 competencies like how well a candidate leads others, manages priorities or provides exceptional service.
While some AI interviews allow candidates to redo their answers, experts suggest recording practice runs to be ready.
This can help you identify bad habits. Perhaps you look away or fidget when you’re nervous, accidentally let slang slip into your speech or spend too much time getting to the point. With apps like Zoom or Google Meet, you can record yourself answering a couple of practice questions. Then review and adjust, Kirk Holland suggests.
Sydell of Modern Hire said candidates should try to fully explain their answers but practice being concise.
“The more detailed you can be the better,” he said. “Don’t ramble. Be to the point.”
Talking to a camera can feel awkward. To help, put up a photo of someone you care about near your camera, Kirk Holland suggests. Then speak directly to them, which should help you display a warmer disposition, make more eye contact and possibly even crack a smile — all of which could be assessed by the AI.
Interview.ai, for example, says its software scans the video for things like body language, facial emotions and eye contact. HireVue previously used facial analysis software in its interviews but began phasing out the technology in 2020 after complaints that the tech could be biased, is unproven and invasive.
“For the most part, language was more powerful (for the model),” said Lindsey Zuloaga, chief data scientist at HireVue. “So we decided to throw out any non-verbals.”
Modern Hire says in the case of a video interview, its AI only assesses the transcript, aiming to remove the potential for bias. Another provider, Sapia.ai, only applies AI to interviews done via written chats. Video is optional, often only used as the next step for top candidates, and isn’t assessed by AI.
“A lot of customers will say we want to see how this person presents,” said Russell Mikowski, Sapia.ai’s president of North America. “So we’ll ask them to answer one question on video.”
Zuloaga said the best way to think about an AI interview is just as another step in the hiring process, but ultimately a human chooses how much to rely on it.
“AI is the filtering step to help humans,” she said. “Humans make the final hiring decision.”

title: From Sales Enablement To Buyer Enablement. Flowa: An AI Email Flow Disruptor.
text:
I have worked in the B2B Technology and CRM related areas for my entire career and the one nightmare particularly in sales and customer service operations is tracking all the customer interaction touch points that are in everyone’s email. Today, the reality is simply email jungle of disconnected email threads is strangling sales and customer service professionals productivity and impacting their employee happiness and wellbeing.
In addition more often than not email interactions in buyer engagement steps cannot be easily traced, across cross- functional enterprise lines.
We focus so much on Sales Enablement and what is more important is the Buyer Enablement hyper focus simplification and integration collection needs.
To cut through all the email clutter noise impacting the buyer experience new email workflow innovations are needed to do more sense making and simplification insight of the buyer journey using advanced AI methods.
With email volumes exploding world-wide, with over 4 billion daily email users and this number is expected to climb to over 4.6 billion by 2025 (Statista, 2021) and today there are more than 310 billion emails sent and received each day.
The email jungle is literally exploding and the productivity of sales and customer service professionals is increasingly buried in email quagmire.
In addition, Gartner research shows a steady shift of customer preferences from in-person sales interactions to digital channels. B2B buyers spend only 17% of the total purchase journey with sales reps.
Because the average deal involves multiple suppliers, a sales rep gets roughly 5% of a customer’s total purchase time. And 44% of millennials prefer no sales rep interaction at all in a B2B setting.
Gartner has also researched that 80% of B2B buyers have stated their last purchase was too complex and difficult. There are simply too many moving parts: not only has the number of stakeholders involved in the decision making doubled, the variety of resources have multiplied as well. Salespeople today rely on documents, videos, interactive demos, forms, electronic signatures, mutual action plans and more.
This fundamentally means that connecting the fragmented email threads across diverse functions in a more streamlined omni channel experience is a critical success factor to modernize B2B sales and customer service organizations.
In addition, due to the increasing volume of email traffic, B2B sales professionals productivity is plummeting so much that AI intelligence is a viable strategy to revolutionize the buyer journey experience - and it’ about time that we move to a more balanced focus between sales enablement and buyer enablement. Complicating this reality is outdated organizational structures where sales ops and customer ops are separated and reporting to different reporting lines.
Although today the majority of sales professionals try to keep all their sales email threads stored in leading CRM Apps like, Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics, etc. A major gap is that these conversation threads do not capture the buyer’s journey as a unique channel of communication, untangled from all the other sales touch points and emails that happen within a B2B purchasing experience.
Hence, most of the email solutions approaches in the market are from a sales centric lense vs a buyer centric lense.
New early stage innovators challenging the status quo - Meet Flowa.
Flowa just has closed a $1.3M pre-seed to save B2B deals from getting lost in long email threads and their vision is intriguing. I had the chance to interview their Co-Founder, and CEO, Erdem Gelal, about the company’s vision, product innovation and application vision of how AI would be applied to solve the email customer buyer journey challenges.
First, a little more about Flowa’s founding team. As a former Venture Capitalist, and having personally a breadth of experiences in early stage SaaS companies, there is always a positive rule of thumb in backing entrepreneurs that have strong entrepreneurial sales and product development experience. Erdem is joined by Alper Yurder and Oguz Gelal, and are Turkish entrepreneurs based in the UK. They bring together complementary skills and experiences: Erdem is a serial entrepreneur who previously has built an enterprise sales solution, acquired by Groupe UP in 2019. Alper has spent the last decade leading sales teams, delivering $30m in revenue, while Oguz shipped products, leading diverse teams in different regions from Canada to Japan. So their international experiences position them well to think global from the get go.
Backed by Antler, Fuel Ventures, ScaleX Ventures and Logo Ventures, this pre-seed funding round will enable Flowla to hire talent and expand internationally - increasing revenues of companies across Europe in the process. They are also backed by a group of industry insiders from companies like Salesforce.
Flowla’s platform is designed to improve productivity and win rates for revenue teams struggling with profitability during high inflation and slowing growth rates. This funding will allow Flowla to hire new talent and expand into new markets internationally, helping more companies grow revenue in the process.
Used by companies like Deel and Insider, Flowla helps bring all materials, actions and conversations in one place, thus removing any friction between a buyer and seller. Helping teams digitally handhold their prospects toward success, Flowla has proven to increase the speed of sales cycles by up to 50%.
I asked Erdem what he thought was the future of sales and he said: “We believe the future of sales is driven by digital experiences that enable buyers. As competition increases, teams are forced to differentiate not only with the service they provide but also with the way they sell. Helping buyers make informed decisions is the new definition of success and sadly, email threads no longer achieve this. This funding will allow us to realize our ambition to build the de facto medium where B2B sales happens.”
Jed Rose, Partner at Antler further comments that “At a time when all inboxes are flooded by unwanted emails, we see revenue teams find it increasingly difficult to create a single source of truth for their buyer. Flowla fills that gap, from first contact to onboarding”.
Dilek Dayinlarli, Founder and Managing Partner at ScaleX Ventures adds "The world of sales is evolving at a rapid pace, and success in this arena heavily depends on a company's ability to understand and optimize the buyer journey. Flowla is at the forefront of this revolution. We are thrilled to be partnering with such a forward-thinking company.”
I asked Erdem what his vision was for Flowa and he said: “
“Flowla helps B2B revenue teams transform processes into step-by-step digital journeys. Flowla unifies all sales resources, actions and conversations in one link for the buyer, removing any friction and speeding up sales cycles.
“We aim to build the de facto medium where B2B sales happens. We envision a world where B2B sales cycles are 100% digital, collaborative, frictionless, and joyful.”
I was impressed with Flowa’s vision statement as they are declaring a dominant position in becoming a go to standard in the industry and emphasized ease of use and joyfulness - happiness for sales and customer service professionals.
Happiness is so important for all professionals, but leading surveys with millions of people and ask them how satisfied they are with their careers. As it turns out, sales representatives rate their career happiness 2.5 out of 5 stars which puts them in the bottom 5% of careers (Career Explorer) Most organizations measure employee satisfaction in annual surveys or use random pulse surveys which are outdated methods to track joy (uber happy), so connecting the dots with mood and health are equally important to increase joy in a sales professional’s career.
Why is your solution important and what is its value?
“Flowla saves B2B deals from falling into cracks in endless email threads. We transform the sales process into a step-by-step digital journey, unifying all resources, actions, and conversations. This flow becomes a single source of truth for the buyer and speeds up sales cycles by up to 50%”, says Erdem.
What are your early customer advocates saying?
“Flowla helped me transform how I collaborate with my prospects and boosted my reply rates by 46%” says Jennis Ferraz-De Souza, International Expansion Consultant at Deel.
What is always important for me in my research is appreciating the lessons learned that CEO’s are experiencing in building their companies and the lessons learned?
“You need 100 true fans to be successful: in the early days of a business, all you need is 100 true fans that love your product, talk about it to others, give feedback, and jump on calls. True growth is possible through this foundation of early supporters. Focusing on building this audience creates a team-wide “user-centric” approach, which is a must have when building a business from scratch.
Minimum disruption to existing workflow: The majority of decision makers are unwilling to add a new solution to their existing stack. The path to adoption is possible with minimum (or zero) disruption to existing workflows.
That’s why we’re heavily invested in integrations with CRM systems, sales engagement solutions, diverse set of content & media types, video solutions and more”, says Erdem.
How are you using AI methods to advance your Flowa IP positioning?
“We’re using OpenAI’s generative model, (aka ChatGPT API) to generate complete flows from scratch, and suggest sections to flows based on the existing flow context. We’ve already built the integration with GPT-3.5 turbo model, will also be adding support for GPT-4 once available. This lets us empower revenue teams to build better narratives and stand out from the competition. Moreover, we’re integrating with ElevenLab’s to create AI-powered realistic speech synthesis to automate adding audio notes to the flows, says Erdem.
In any emerging new SaaS company, differentiation is critical, so I asked Erdem who he felt his top competitors were and what was unique about Flowa?
“We’re disrupting the legacy “sales enablement” space dominated by unicorn players like Seismic, Highspot, through: focusing on the buyer’s experience instead of the seller and growing with a bottoms up approach instead of tops down, with a more accessible price point. This new category we target is referred to as Buyer Enablement. The majority of entrants focus on helping sellers build “mini websites” that focus on bringing different materials together. We see the real value lies in transforming these different materials into a “workflow” with built in automation rules and AI guidance,” says Erdem.
Buyer enablement is the provisioning of information that supports the completion of critical activities necessary to make a purchase. “Just as sales enablement helps sellers sell, buyer enablement helps buyers buy by providing them with prescriptive advice and practical support to make the buying process easier to navigate and complete” (Gartner Group)
Of course I had to ask Erdem, if he felt Salesforce was already doing what Flowa was doing? His thoughts were intriguing.
“CRM systems are internal solutions focusing on centralizing, tracking and reporting customer & revenue data. Flowa is building a digital experience for the buyer, which is fully integrated to the CRM. For every opportunity in Salesforce, there exists a corresponding “flow” built with Flowla. One is the seller’s single source of truth while the other one is the buyer’s. This is also why we have an angel investor who is a VP at Salesforce,” says Erdem.
Conclusion:
The increasing shift to buyer enablement from sales enablement in 2023 and beyond will continue to intensify. With productivity declines plummeting with B2B sales and customer service professionals being buried in administrative overheads, much of it is attributed to email overloads and the jungle of email threads distributed across different sales and customer service interactions.
To date, already the median B2B buying group involves six to 10 decision makers‚ each armed with four or five pieces of information they have gathered for themselves (Gartner Group).
Flowa has tremendous market and growth potential, and their vision focused on “Joy” is a rallying brand positioning opportunity where sales professionals mental health, well being and job satisfaction is increasingly worrisome, as I have written about extensively over the past year on the declining happiness risks. To Read my happiness research here and here.
Finding pathways to restructure workflow logic intelligently to separate out internal communications from customers centric communication into a unified buyer journey workflow makes tremendous business sense.
Making this process ‘dead simple” will be critical as sales professionals are already overloaded with sales stack fatigue with many productivity enablement apps - so it will be key that Chief Revenue Operational Leaders ensure new investments include resourcing in change management to ensure they can support and monitor how sales professionals are shifting their behaviors in using their CRM’s - to work within a pre-defined workflow enablement layer vs hide in their own silos (which is very easy to do as a B2B sales professional).
Flowa is cracking a strategic gap in the B2B Sales SaaS ecosystem, but from my early research and discussions with Erdem and some of the key investors, this team has a clear vision, early customer validation and a winning attitude to make a difference to put joy on more sales professionals faces - and if that’s not a motivating vision - I don’t know what is.
Every sales and customer service professional deserves more happiness to escape the email jungle entanglements that they are experiencing daily.
Flowa is a market disruptor to be tried and cheered on. It takes a tremendous amount of courage to tackle a very crowded sales software ecosystem - but sellers must improve their B2B sales productivity as the administrative burdens are strangling their focus on what’s really important and that is speaking to more customers.
I look forward to interviewing Erdem in twelve months to check in on Flowa’s commercialization progress and wish his team, and investors a successful pre-seed growth trajectory.

title: Council Post: How Can AI Fit Into Customer Service Call Centers Effectively?
text:
Jennifer Lee is Chief Operating Officer at Intradiem. She’s also a yogi, a mother and a tenacious advocate for women in technology.
When I started my first job in a call center 20 years ago, people were already talking about how technology and automated processes were on the verge of replacing human agents. Today, with artificial intelligence (AI) blossoming in every direction, that familiar refrain about technology replacing human agents is stronger than ever.
Except that it won’t. Not yet, at least.
No matter how fast and smart technology becomes, it will never be a satisfying substitute for a human-to-human connection during high-stakes moments of truth in customer interactions. Automation is great when we need to schedule an appointment or make a payment. But when it comes to things like disputing a hospital bill, filing an insurance claim or committing to a long-term purchase agreement, there’s nothing like the real thing.
Companies Often Misuse AI Programs And Models
Unfortunately, some contact center leaders are repeating errors made with early chatbots by viewing the current generation of AI applications as straight-on replacements for human capabilities. Predictably, this is causing a power struggle between people and machines.
The Wall Street Journal (paywall) published an article that describes how some call centers are using machine-learning models to take decision-making responsibility away from agents. For example, they're scanning conversations and recommending what agents should say or do next based on words and sentiments expressed by customers. But agents are pushing back.
Many agents interviewed said they value AI’s ability to access information quickly for decision making, but they object to being forced to use AI-generated scripts against their own judgment. They'd rather trust their own judgment when it comes to the inherently emotional aspect of customer service, especially since AI assistants can still make errors.
A quick perusal of the WSJ article’s comment section makes it clear that customers aren’t fans either. They want their problems solved with the nuance and empathy that only a human can provide.
AI Can Help Agents Improve, Not Replace Them
Technology really does affect the way human beings work. But customer service isn't a zero-sum game where additional input from technology must come at the expense of human workers. It’s not about how to divide the pie; it’s about how to expand it.
Automation of key contact center processes in recent years has streamlined workflow efficiency, but it hasn’t improved agents’ ability to satisfy customers once they’re connected. Why? Because they’re still handling direct customer engagement and also processing and interpreting the inputs needed to resolve customer problems.
Rather than replacing human workers, technologies like ChatGPT and other AI applications will change the way some jobs are done. That’s not a threat. It’s an opportunity and a great one at that. The way to get the most from this tech in the contact center is to use AI’s uniquely powerful capabilities to assume the transactional and processing tasks it can do better than humans. This additional support can help agents get better and faster at delivering moments of truth.
In a fraction of the time it takes a human agent, AI can access and process huge pools of data, identify relevant patterns and predict the best solution to whatever problem is at hand. This collapses delay and inefficiency, retrieving and collating critical missing information and placing it at the agent’s disposal instantaneously. AI support liberates agents so they can remain focused on applying nuanced judgment—a uniquely human ability—based on the urgency of the situation, the comfort level of the customer and other variables.
AI Complements Human Intelligence
We all want our customer service experiences to be more efficient, and AI can help make it so without losing our primal need for compassion at high-stakes moments. We recognize the reassurance in a firm handshake, a steady gaze and the cadence of a confident voice. We know it when we feel it and when we don’t. AI may get there one day, but until it does, we should focus on leveraging its enormous potential to complement our finely honed intelligence.
As AI continues to mature, contact centers should keep routing transactional and computational tasks to chatbots while reserving more complex requests for human agents. These companies can provide stronger support to agents through applications specifically designed to streamline training, coaching, time and stress management and other steps to boost agents’ skills and well-being.
Customer service is a quintessentially human domain where promises to deliver outcomes or rectify mistakes are premised on a bedrock of faith, so people will always play a decisive role. Despite AI’s awesome ability to fill in the gaps of our deficiencies, there’s still no algorithm for faith. So its role in call centers should be a highly effective support tool that allows agents to better satisfy customers' needs.

title: Council Post: How Marketers Can Leverage AI In Search Engines
text:
Founder & CEO of Angora Media, a TLV-based digital marketing agency with a mission to deliver high quality leads and sales to our clients.
As AI technology continues to evolve, understanding how it works is essential for marketers looking to get ahead of the competition.
By understanding how AI search works, marketers can leverage its potential and create more effective marketing campaigns, optimize their content for search engine visibility and drive higher traffic from targeted audiences. With its predictive capabilities and personalized recommendations, AI can help marketers identify the best-performing strategies that will generate maximum returns on investment.
How AI Assists With Search Results
Bing has recently made headlines for incorporating OpenAI into its search engine. Baidu, too, has announced an AI-powered search engine. And since 2015, Google has used AI to help rank web pages based on their relevance to a given query.
Initially, the rankings were done using a combination of human curators called "quality raters" and algorithms. Quality raters still help Google categorize information to improve its systems.
With time, though, companies like Google have been relying more on algorithms to rank web pages since they are able to process more data and are also able to update rankings more quickly when new information becomes available.
Here are two main areas where AI assists Google with search results.
• Quality Control: Google’s search algorithm is programmed to act like a human and decide what the best content for any given search query is. The algorithm is trained to take into account different factors such as word choice, readability and length in order to provide accurate results.
• Understand Search Queries: The search engine AI is useful for understanding how people search for pages and inferring what users are searching for on their search engines. The algorithm is designed to generate results that will best match the intent of the user and provide personalized responses to queries.
AI Algorithms Google Uses To Rank Pages
1. RankBrain
RankBrain is a machine learning algorithm that was introduced by Google in 2015. It is one of the ranking factors and went from affecting approximately 15% of global queries in 2015 to all of them. It helps understand important words in natural language and extract the key meaning of sentences to make accurate predictions about what a search result might be about. It is said to be especially adept at novel inquiries.
2. BERT
Neural matching algorithms help create models for finding meaningful patterns in data. This allows for a better understanding of how queries relate to pages. By using statistical and neural machine learning theories, it compares new input to past input and predicts an output.
Specifically, Google has developed a "neural network-based technique for natural language processing (NLP)" called BERT, officially introduced in 2019, which is said to be better than human copywriters at producing creative, accurate content.
It works by creating a mathematical representation of the input text and then choosing the best output with the help of a machine-learning system. This algorithm helps Google understand how combinations of words express different intents and meanings.
3. MUM (Multitask Unified Model)
MUM is one of Google's latest AI milestones in search, and it is cited by the company as being "1,000 times more powerful than BERT." MUM can take advantage of everything from structured information like data tables to unstructured data such as text, images and video.
It is also capable of both understanding and generating content across 75 languages at the same time. This allows it to develop a more comprehensive understanding of information and world knowledge.
Five Best Practices For Marketers Using AI-Based Search Engine Optimization
1. Don't over-optimize your website content.
Search engines like Google put a lot of focus on how the content on a website is written and structured to ensure its relevance in the search results.
It still doesn't ensure that it will be seen, though. This is where SEO strategies come into play. An SEO strategy should not just be focused on content but also on other factors like site structure, quality of links and social signals and mentions.
2. Don't target too broad of terms.
Generally speaking, it's best not to target too broad of terms with the hope that your site will rank for those terms later on. There are exceptions to this rule, though, such as if you have to rank for a pet term or industry term that you can't target specifically.
3. Keep mobile searches in mind.
Mobile users are likely to make up an increasing share of the total search queries. Search engines are now more likely to prioritize sites that offer their content in a mobile-friendly format.
4. Use high-quality, original content.
Modern search engines are more likely to rank your site higher if the content on it is relevant, useful and high quality. Make sure that your site has an eye-catching title tag in addition to metadata, keyword-rich text and well-written, informative content.
5. Create content that is helpful and useful.
In December, Google released a helpful content update that sends out signals to be picked up by automated ranking systems. This helps guarantee that people can find helpful and unique content that was written with them in mind when they do a search.
The Future Of Artificial Intelligence For Search Engines
As AI and machine learning continue to develop and improve, their application in search engine algorithms is becoming more and more prominent. This could potentially revolutionize how users search for content and how marketers promote businesses online.
We can anticipate more accurate, personalized results as the future of artificial intelligence for search engines progresses. However, marketers should note that this also has the potential to create some concerns. If these algorithms are not properly monitored and overseen, they could produce a biased industry.
This is yet another reason to learn how this technology works when it comes to your content.

title: Council Post: Building An AI Plan? 13 Tech Experts Share Strategies For Success
text:
As artificial intelligence continues to revolutionize the ways we live and work, businesses of all sizes are grappling with the question of whether they need an AI plan. While some may argue that AI is only relevant to tech-focused companies, the reality is that, with its ever-evolving capabilities and ever-growing number of applications, AI is becoming enormously impactful across a wide range of industries and is increasingly a “must-have” part of most companies’ tech foundations.
However, there’s no fixed template for incorporating AI; leaders in every business must carefully explore their unique needs and goals before developing an AI plan. Below, 13 Forbes Technology Council members provide their expert insights into how interested businesses can go about creating an AI plan that will boost their productivity and competitive edge.
1. Consider How AI Can Meet Your Specific Business Needs
AI is here to stay. Whether you have a specific AI plan or it is a division of your overall strategy, having a plan is important to determine how it can help with productivity. The key lies in how AI can help your business specifically. First analyze how it can generate value for your business, solve any stress points or reduce costs. Don’t just follow the trend; think critically about how it can support you. - Pete Hanlon, Moneypenny
2. See Where AI Can Add Value
AI is quickly becoming a competitive advantage in all industries. Companies should identify use cases where AI can add value, assess their data readiness and ensure ethical AI practices. It’s also important to invest in talent, partnerships and technologies to implement AI solutions. Businesses that fail to adopt AI risk falling behind competitors and missing out on the efficiency and cost savings AI can offer. - Kuk Jiang, ZEGOCLOUD PTE. LTD
Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
3. Define Your Goals, Assess Your Data And Build A Plan
The benefits of AI are not limited to a specific set of industries. Hometown little league coaches can use AI to create new sports plays. Large enterprises such as the Department of Defense are using AI to build preventative maintenance programs for military equipment. Start your AI journey by defining your goals, assessing your data infrastructure and building an iterative implementation plan. - Shawn Wells, Mission IT
4. Focus On These Five Areas
When developing an AI plan, the biggest areas to focus on are: 1. defining high-level business goals and measurable outcomes, 2. identifying and assessing internal and external data sources for accuracy and completeness, 3. defining, stacking, ranking and prioritizing AI and machine learning use cases, 4. building and piloting models, and 5. reassessing the pilot models, measuring, testing, learning and consistently iterating. - Mathew Cagney, Renewtrak
5. Ensure Thorough Data Management Practices And Cybersecurity Measures Are In Place
A well-designed AI plan should identify areas of the business that are suited for AI; establish ethical and transparent usage practices, confidentiality, privacy and security; and invest in employee education. With thorough data management practices and cybersecurity measures in place, a responsible and successful AI implementation can deliver long-term value. - Avani Desai, Schellman
6. Determine If AI Will Be Used For Internal Or Customer-Facing Processes (Or Both)
AI is already part of everyone’s lives and companies—it impacts a business’ online presence, marketing reach, how it builds a talent pool via online platforms and more. That said, AI can be utilized effectively to improve the outcomes within every company too. The first step would be for company leaders to define whether they want to implement it internally for productivity and efficiency, make it part of their offerings to their customers or both. - Arungalai Anbarasu, Waygate Technologies - a Baker Hughes Business
7. Consider How Human Ingenuity Could Be Augmented By Machine Intelligence
To say that every company needs an AI plan is an exaggeration; however, every company should have at least an awareness of AI. Think creatively about how human ingenuity and machine intelligence can partner to make your products and services more meaningful. It would be shortsighted not to understand where AI is going and how that might disrupt your business or make it better. - Christopher Rogers, Carenet Health
8. Be Prepared For A Learning Curve
AI sounds very futuristic, but it’s here, and it’s not going anywhere. The first step in developing an AI plan is to identify your core business needs. Then, identify AI technologies that address your use cases. AI can make existing processes faster, more efficient and automated; however, it takes time to be learned and harnessed for the greatest impact. Make sure employees are educated on any new tools. - Austin Gadient, Vali Cyber
9. Invest In The Talent For Continuous Iteration
Every company needs an AI plan to stay competitive. AI is transforming the way companies operate, and not incorporating AI in strategies could lead to a company’s falling behind. To develop an AI strategy, a company should define its vision, assess its readiness, identify use cases, create a roadmap, address ethics and safety, invest in talent and continuously evaluate and iterate. - Soumyarka Mondal, Sybill Inc.
10. Create An Ethics Framework For AI Use In Marketing Or Human Resources
AI is revolutionizing the way businesses operate, with marketing, websites and recruiting being the latest focuses. There is a growing concern about the ethics of using AI in these areas. Are recruiting platforms and algorithms embedding learned biases? It is important to have an AI ethics framework in marketing and human resources as more AI is used internally or through vendors. - Tracy Levine, SonKsuru
11. Seek Guidance From Experts
Creating an AI plan is crucial for companies to remain competitive in today’s business landscape. The plan should outline goals, data sources and AI tools and provide clear guidelines for ethical and responsible AI use. Seeking guidance from experts in the field is critical. Challenges aside, AI offers significant benefits and is a necessary consideration for every company. - Imane Adel, Paymob
12. Consider The Possibilities In Terms Of Revenue And Competitive Advantage
Not every company necessarily needs an AI plan, as it depends on the nature of the business and the strategic goals of the organization. However, in today’s rapidly changing technological landscape, more and more companies are recognizing that implementing AI can lead to improved efficiency, increased revenue and a competitive advantage in the marketplace. - Nicole Lytle, Craftly.AI
13. Consider AI As Part Of An Overall Innovation And Technical Plan
As engaging as AI is (and I was an AI research leader in the 1980s), it does not deserve its own plan. The last thing an information-overloaded organization needs is a plan for every promising technology that emerges. I do, however, subscribe to an overall innovation and technical plan that identifies a portfolio of emerging technologies an organization is looking to prioritize and invest in. - Laurence Lock Lee, Swoop Analytics
